segments.voice: Last week ended in the Devi Mahatmya with one syllable, hum, and Kali springing from the goddess's own brow, named Chamunda. A new week begins.

Every drop. That's the problem in the eighth chapter. His generals dead, Shumbha sends out his whole army, and something new happens. From the bodies of the gods, their powers step out, each a goddess in that god's own form. From Brahma, one on a swan, with prayer beads and a water pot. From Shiva, one on a bull, holding a trident. From Vishnu, one on Garuda, the great bird. From Indra, one on an elephant, with a thunderbolt. A boar-faced goddess. A lion-faced goddess. They gather around the goddess. Then a demon walks out to meet them: Raktabija. Blood-Seed.
screen: `SHUMBHA SENDS HIS WHOLE ARMY.` → `THE GODS' POWERS STEP OUT.` → `A DEMON NAMED BLOOD-SEED.`

segments.voice: First the goddess does something surprising. From her own body comes one more power, fierce, howling like a pack of jackals, and she gives Shiva himself a job: go to Shumbha and Nishumbha as my messenger. Give heaven back and go home to the underworld, or come and fight. Because Shiva was her messenger, she's called Shivaduti. The demons choose to fight. Then Raktabija. His power is in his name: whenever a drop of his blood falls to the ground, a new demon rises from it, just as strong. The goddesses strike him with thunderbolt, spear, discus, trident, and each wound makes it worse. Soon the field is full of him, and the gods are terrified. So the goddess, smiling, turns to Kali. In paraphrase: open your mouth wide, and take in every drop before it touches the ground. Kali does. As the goddess strikes, Kali drinks the blood and swallows the new demons as they rise. The drops stop landing. Drained, Raktabija falls. Notice what wins. Not a bigger weapon; every weapon only made more of him. What wins is catching the thing before it can grow again. Some readers hear in Raktabija the way a resentment or a craving multiplies each time it's fed. The text leaves that open. What it shows is Kali's open mouth, and a field that finally empties.
screen: `SHIVA SENT AS HER MESSENGER.` · `EVERY DROP BECOMES A DEMON.` · `EACH WOUND MAKES IT WORSE.` · `KALI CATCHES EVERY DROP.` · then, large: `DON'T LET THE DROPS LAND.`

segments.voice: Let a small irritation come to mind and watch one thought grow from it, then another: that's the multiplying. Gently go back to the first one, without feeding or fighting it, and let it settle on the breath out before it can land; if it multiplies again, come back again. If you pray, ask for help in your own words; if you don't, let the breath be what catches it.
The Devi Mahatmya. Today, its eighth chapter: the gods' powers as goddesses, Shiva sent as a messenger, and Raktabija, beaten when Kali caught every drop.
Your line: the Devi Mahatmya, read whole. Every weapon made more of him; an open mouth caught the drops. A new week, well begun.

howItsDone: The goddesses who come out of the gods in the eighth chapter are known together as the Matrikas, the Mothers, and groups of them are carved and worshiped in some Hindu temples.

original.note: Sanskrit: rakta-bīja, blood-seed. The demon whose every drop of blood becomes another of him.

notes: First day of week two of year four. Chapter 8 paraphrased: the śaktis of Brahma (on a swan, rosary and water pot), Maheshvara (on a bull, trident), Kumara (peacock, spear; not named in the voice), Vishnu (on Garuda), Varahi (boar form), Narasimhi (lion form), Indra (thunderbolt, on Airavata). The text names more forms; the script names some. Confirm.
Chandika's own śakti, howling like jackals, sends Shiva as messenger (give back the three worlds and go to Pātāla, or fight); hence Śivadūtī. Confirm.
Raktabija: each drop of blood falling to earth produces an asura equal to him; Kali drinks the blood and devours the new ones; he falls bloodless. Confirm.
'Some readers hear in Raktabija the way a resentment or a craving multiplies' is attributed interpretation; confirm a Keeper is comfortable.
